title: Indexes
subtitle: B-tree, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, partial indexes, and when not to index
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: A table with 10 million rows and no index on the email column requires PostgreSQL to read all 10 million rows to find one user by email — a sequential scan. This takes seconds. With a B-tree index, the same lookup takes milliseconds by jumping directly to the matching row.
whyItExists.solution: Indexes are separate data structures that let PostgreSQL find rows quickly without scanning the whole table. The tradeoff: indexes make reads faster but writes slower (the index must be updated too).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Index foreign key columns, columns used in WHERE clauses, columns used in ORDER BY when combined with LIMIT, and columns used as JOIN keys.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Small tables (< ~1000 rows) — sequential scan is fast enough. Columns with very low cardinality (boolean, small enum) where the index would select half the table anyway. Write-heavy tables with minimal reads.

content.code:
-- See the query plan without running
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';

-- Run the query and show actual timing
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';

-- Show buffer usage (cache hits vs disk reads)
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';

-- Reading the output:
--   Seq Scan  → reading every row (bad for large tables + selective filter)
--   Index Scan → using an index to find rows (fast for selective queries)
--   Index Only Scan → all needed data is in the index itself (fastest)
--   Bitmap Heap Scan → fetches blocks of matching rows (batch of index lookups)

-- Cost format: (startup cost..total cost) (rows=estimate) (width=bytes per row)
-- Index Scan using idx_users_email on users  (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=1 width=136)
--   (actual time=0.045..0.046 rows=1 loops=1)

content.text: The most impactful indexes: (1) Foreign key columns, (2) columns in WHERE clauses on large tables, (3) columns in ORDER BY when used with LIMIT. Adding all three will fix the majority of slow queries in a typical web application.

questions.question: You have a composite index on (user_id, status). Which query CAN use this index?
options: ORDER BY created_at (not in the index)
questions.explanation: Composite indexes can be used for queries on the leftmost column(s). WHERE user_id = 5 uses the first column of (user_id, status) and will use the index. WHERE status = 'active' alone skips the leftmost column and will NOT use this index (PostgreSQL will do a Seq Scan unless another index exists on status).

faq.q: How do I find which queries are slow?
faq.a: Enable pg_stat_statements (CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements) to track query performance statistics. Query: SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10; — shows the slowest average queries. Then run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on those queries to see what plan they are using.

examples: A startup's 'user lookup by email' query went from 2 seconds to 0.5ms after adding CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email) — single most impactful database change
Partial indexes on status columns are common: WHERE status != 'completed' indexes only active records, staying small even as the completed orders table grows to millions of rows
